    theorem OspOddDeformations.General.intertwine_map.{u_1, u_2, u_3} {B : Type u_1}
  [Fintype B] {R : Type u_2} {S : Type u_3} [CommRing R] [CommRing S]
  (φ : R →+* S) (c c' : B → B → B → R) (t : B → B → R)
  (h :
    ∀ (p q : B),
      OspOddDeformations.General.bilOf c (t p) (t q) =
        OspOddDeformations.General.linOf t (c' p q))
  (x y : B → S) :
  OspOddDeformations.General.bilOf (fun p q => ⇑φ ∘ c p q)
      (OspOddDeformations.General.linOf (fun p => ⇑φ ∘ t p) x)
      (OspOddDeformations.General.linOf (fun p => ⇑φ ∘ t p) y) =
    OspOddDeformations.General.linOf (fun p => ⇑φ ∘ t p)
      (OspOddDeformations.General.bilOf (fun p q => ⇑φ ∘ c' p q) x y)
    theorem OspOddDeformations.General.intertwine_map.{u_1,
    u_2, u_3}
  {B : Type u_1} [Fintype B]
  {R : Type u_2} {S : Type u_3}
  [CommRing R] [CommRing S] (φ : R →+* S)
  (c c' : B → B → B → R) (t : B → B → R)
  (h :
    ∀ (p q : B),
      OspOddDeformations.General.bilOf c
          (t p) (t q) =
        OspOddDeformations.General.linOf t
          (c' p q))
  (x y : B → S) :
  OspOddDeformations.General.bilOf
      (fun p q => ⇑φ ∘ c p q)
      (OspOddDeformations.General.linOf
        (fun p => ⇑φ ∘ t p) x)
      (OspOddDeformations.General.linOf
        (fun p => ⇑φ ∘ t p) y) =
    OspOddDeformations.General.linOf
      (fun p => ⇑φ ∘ t p)
      (OspOddDeformations.General.bilOf
        (fun p q => ⇑φ ∘ c' p q) x y)
    An intertwining `bilOf c (T e_p) (T e_q) = T (bilOf c' e_p e_q)` over `R`, with `T = linOf t`,
gives `bilOf (φc) (T_φ x) (T_φ y) = T_φ (bilOf (φc') x y)` over `S` for all `x y : B → S`.

    theorem OspOddDeformations.OspN.Gamma_eq_delta_fBeta
  (F : OspOddDeformations.OspN.FermionIndex) (n : ℕ)
  (x y : OspOddDeformations.OspN.OspMod F n) :
  OspOddDeformations.OspN.Gamma x y =
    OspOddDeformations.OspN.delta (OspOddDeformations.OspN.fBeta F n) x
      y
    theorem OspOddDeformations.OspN.Gamma_eq_delta_fBeta
  (F :
    OspOddDeformations.OspN.FermionIndex)
  (n : ℕ)
  (x y :
    OspOddDeformations.OspN.OspMod F n) :
  OspOddDeformations.OspN.Gamma x y =
    OspOddDeformations.OspN.delta
      (OspOddDeformations.OspN.fBeta F n)
      x y
    **`Γ_β = δf_β`** (paper Theorem 4.7, its main clause). Since `f_β = h̃ − ad Z_β`
pointwise, `deltaBasis`'s own three-term formula (built from `bracket0` and one direct
application of `f`) distributes over that subtraction termwise (`bracket0_sub_left`/
`_right`, `smul_sub`), giving `δh̃ = δf_β + δ(ad Z_β)` at the basis level, hence at the
general level after summing. `δ(ad Z_β) = 0` by `delta_ad_eq_zero`,
using `Zbeta_odd` for the oddness side condition.
Combined with `Gamma_eq_delta_hTilde` (already proved), `Γ = δh̃ = δf_β + 0 = δf_β`.

    theorem OspOddDeformations.OspN.Gamma_eq_delta_hTilde
  {F : OspOddDeformations.OspN.FermionIndex} {n : ℕ}
  (x y : OspOddDeformations.OspN.OspMod F n) :

    theorem OspOddDeformations.OspN.Gamma_eq_delta_hTilde
  {F :
    OspOddDeformations.OspN.FermionIndex}
  {n : ℕ}
  (x y :
    OspOddDeformations.OspN.OspMod F n) :
  OspOddDeformations.OspN.Gamma x y =
    OspOddDeformations.OspN.delta
      OspOddDeformations.OspN.hTilde x y
    **`Γ_β = δh̃`**, the bilinear extension to arbitrary elements of `OspMod F n`:
`Gamma`/`delta` are both literally the same double sum shape against
`GammaBasis`/`deltaBasis hTilde`, which now agree termwise by
`Gamma_eq_delta_hTilde_basis`.

  {F : OspOddDeformations.OspN.FermionIndex} {n r : ℕ}
  (Y : OspOddDeformations.OspN.Multi.RModM F n r)
  (hY : OspOddDeformations.OspN.Presented.HomM 0 Y)
  (x z : OspOddDeformations.OspN.Multi.RModM F n r) :
  OspOddDeformations.OspN.Multi.bracket0M Y
      (OspOddDeformations.OspN.Multi.bracket0M x z) =

        (OspOddDeformations.OspN.Multi.bracket0M Y x) z +
      OspOddDeformations.OspN.Multi.bracket0M x
        (OspOddDeformations.OspN.Multi.bracket0M Y z)
    theorem OspOddDeformations.OspN.GroupB.bracket0M_derivation
  {F :
    OspOddDeformations.OspN.FermionIndex}
  {n r : ℕ}
  (Y :
    OspOddDeformations.OspN.Multi.RModM F
      n r)
  (hY :
    OspOddDeformations.OspN.Presented.HomM
      0 Y)
  (x z :
    OspOddDeformations.OspN.Multi.RModM F
      n r) :
  OspOddDeformations.OspN.Multi.bracket0M
      Y
      (OspOddDeformations.OspN.Multi.bracket0M

    OspOddDeformations.OspN.Multi.bracket0M
        (OspOddDeformations.OspN.Multi.bracket0M

          Y z)

          (OspOddDeformations.OspN.Multi.bracketBetaM
            (OspOddDeformations.OspN.Multi.eM

Remark 5.7 (The Fock module). In this remark k,l run over \{1,\ldots,n\}. Let \mathcal F=R_r[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathrm{Cl}(N), with the x_k even and \mathrm{Cl}(N) acting on itself by left multiplication. Sending B_{2k-1}\mapsto\partial_{x_k} and B_{2k}\mapsto x_k represents A_0 on \mathcal F, and composing with \Phi_r represents A_\beta, faithfully, as in the case N=1, r=1 of [Aoi26]. For N=n=r=1 this is the Fock space of [BS17, Section 4], where the mixed relation is realized by an odd derivation and the annihilated element is 1 (see [Aoi26]). Put \eta_{kl}=\Theta_{(2k-1)(2l-1)} and \zeta_{kl}=\Theta_{(2k-1)(2l)}. Since \Theta is \mathbb I plus a matrix with entries of \kappa-degree at least 2, so is \eta, and \eta is invertible. Put \Xi=\eta^{-1}\zeta and \tilde c_k=\sum_l(\eta^{-1})_{kl}c_{2l-1}, and let \Xi^+ and \Xi^- be the symmetric and antisymmetric parts of \Xi. The elements annihilated by every b_{2k-1} are exactly the \varpi\,\sigma with \sigma\in R_r\otimes\mathrm{Cl}(N), where

\varpi=\exp\Bigl(-\tfrac12\sum_{k,l}\Xi^+_{kl}x_kx_l-\sum_kx_k\tilde c_k\Bigr),

a finite sum. Indeed, \mathfrak b_k=\sum_l(\eta^{-1})_{kl}b_{2l-1} acts as \partial_{x_k}+\sum_l\Xi_{kl}x_l+\tilde c_k, and the \mathfrak b_k commute, since J_{(2k-1)(2l-1)}=0. This gives [\tilde c_k,\tilde c_l]=2\Xi^-_{kl}, a central scalar. With \xi=\sum_kx_k\tilde c_k, one has \partial_{x_k}e^{-\xi}=-(\tilde c_k-\tfrac12[\xi,\tilde c_k])e^{-\xi}. The Gaussian factor \exp(-\tfrac12\sum_{k,l}\Xi^+_{kl}x_kx_l) is central in \mathcal F, and \partial_{x_k} multiplies it by -(\Xi^+x)_k, which absorbs the symmetric part of \Xi. The \tilde c_k act by left multiplication. The antisymmetric part \Xi^- cancels the term \tfrac12[\xi,\tilde c_k]=-(\Xi^-x)_k, which arises because the \tilde c_k do not commute. So \mathfrak b_k\varpi=0. Conversely, \varpi is invertible, and \mathfrak b_k(\varpi\sigma')=\varpi\,\partial_{x_k}\sigma' for every \sigma'\in\mathcal F. With \Omega^{\mathrm{oo}}_{kl}=\Omega_{(2k-1)(2l-1)}, \Omega^{\mathrm{oe}}_{kl}=\Omega_{(2k-1)(2l)} and c_{\mathrm o}=(c_{2k-1})_k, the table below lists the cases worked out. In it, \theta, f and \lambda are even central elements of R_r.

\begin{array}{llll} \text{case} & \Theta & \Xi & \varpi \\ \hline r=1 & \mathbb I & 0 & 1-\sum_kx_kc_{2k-1} \\ r=2 & \mathbb I+\tfrac12\Omega J & \tfrac12\Omega^{\mathrm{oo}} & \exp(-\sum_kx_kc_{2k-1}) \\ r=3 & \mathbb I+\tfrac12\Omega J & \tfrac12\Omega^{\mathrm{oo}} & \exp(-\sum_kx_k\tilde c_k) \text{,} \tilde c=(\mathbb I+\tfrac12\Omega^{\mathrm{oe}})c_{\mathrm o} \\ n=1 & \theta\,\mathbb I & 0 & \exp(-\theta^{-1}x_1c_1) \\ N=1 & \mathbb I+f\,\Omega J & \lambda\,(\gamma_{2k-1,0}\gamma_{2l-1,0})_{kl} & \exp(-\sum_kx_k\tilde c_k) \end{array}

For r=2, \eta^{-1}=\mathbb I+\tfrac12\Omega^{\mathrm{oe}} and \Omega^{\mathrm{oe}}c_{\mathrm o} has \kappa-degree 3, so \tilde c=c_{\mathrm o}. For n=1, \Omega=\omega J and \Theta=(1-\omega)^{1/2}\mathbb I. For N=1, (\Omega J)^2 is an even multiple of \Omega J, which gives the form of \Theta. The Gaussian factor \exp(-\tfrac12\sum_{k,l}\Xi^+_{kl}x_kx_l) is 1 unless N,n\geq2 and r\geq4. Indeed, \Xi^+=0 in three cases. For r\leq3, \Theta=\mathbb I+\tfrac12\Omega J and \Xi=\tfrac12(\Omega_{(2k-1)(2l-1)})_{kl}, which is antisymmetric. For n=1, \Theta is a multiple of \mathbb I, so \zeta=0 and \Xi=0. Let \Theta=(\mathbb I+\Omega J)^{1/2}=\sum_{k\geq0}\binom{1/2}{k}(\Omega J)^k, a finite sum ending at k=\lfloor r/2\rfloor, since the entries of (\Omega J)^k have \kappa-degree 2k. Eq.{u_1} {α : Sort u_1} : α → α → PropThe equality relation. It has one introduction rule, `Eq.refl`. We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`. A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation. ``` variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α) variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d) example : a = d := Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd ``` Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value. That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`. Example: ``` example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop) (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b := Eq.subst h1 h2 example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop) (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b := h1 ▸ h2 ``` The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
